title: Time Strategy and How to Attack Every Question
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Start here
summary: A time plan for every module, the two-pass method, a five-step attack for every question, and the seven trap-answer families that catch most students.

blocks.text: Knowing English well is not enough on the Digital SAT. You also need a plan for the clock and a fixed way of attacking every question, so that you never panic, never waste three minutes on one item, and never fall for the same trap twice. This page gives you that plan.
What this page trains

Every Reading and Writing module gives you **27 questions in 32 minutes** — about **1 minute 11 seconds per question**. Two of the 27 are unscored pretest questions, but you cannot tell which, so all 27 deserve an answer. There is **no penalty for wrong answers**, and inside a module you can move back and forth and **mark questions for review**. You cannot go back to Module 1 once Module 2 starts. These four facts are the base of the whole strategy.
1. Your time budget

Not every question needs 71 seconds. Grammar questions are often answered in 30–45 seconds once you know the rules; inference, evidence and two-passage questions may need 90 seconds or more. The idea is to **save time on the fast questions so you can spend it on the slow ones**.

rows: You test the choices against a rule; often you only need the sentence around the blank.
Read the sentence before the blank and the sentence with the blank; decide the relationship.
Short passage; predict a word, then match.
Read the goal first; most choices can be eliminated without reading all the notes again.
You must understand the whole passage.
Several steps of logic; the slowest group.
First pass finished; now return to marked questions

blocks.title: Use the clock, do not stare at it
blocks.text: Check the time only at the checkpoints above. Looking at the clock after every question makes you nervous and slower.
2. The two-pass method

items: **First pass:** go through the module in order. Answer every question you can answer with confidence.
If a question is taking more than about **90 seconds** and you are still unsure, eliminate what you can, **choose your best answer anyway**, **mark it for review**, and move on.
Never leave a question blank on the first pass. If time runs out before you return, you still have an answer there.
**Second pass:** use the remaining minutes to return to the marked questions. Often the answer becomes clear when you see the passage again with a fresh mind.
Change an answer on the second pass only if you find a **clear reason in the text**. Do not change answers because of a vague feeling.

blocks.text: Why does this work? A hard question and an easy question are worth the same scored point. If you spend three minutes on one hard question near the start, you may later rush through three easy grammar questions at the end and lose them. The two-pass method protects the easy points first.

blocks.title: طريقة المرّتين (Two-pass)
blocks.text: في المرة الأولى جاوب على كل الأسئلة اللي متأكد منها. لو سؤال أخد منك أكتر من دقيقة ونص: احذف الاختيارات الغلط، اختار أحسن إجابة، اعمل Mark for review وكمّل. في الآخر ارجع للأسئلة المعلّمة. ومتسيبش أي سؤال فاضي أبدًا، لأن مفيش خصم على الإجابة الغلط.
3. The attack method for every question
Use the same five steps every time. After two or three weeks they become automatic.

items: **Read the question stem first.** It tells you the job: a word, the main idea, a logical completion, a grammar rule, a goal from notes. Knowing the job before reading makes your reading focused.
**Read the whole passage.** It is only 25–150 words. Skimming causes most reading mistakes, because the key word (however, only, not, some) is often in the middle.

**Predict the answer in your own words before looking at the choices.** For a blank, think of your own word. For a main idea, say the idea in five to ten words. For a transition, name the relationship (contrast, example, result, addition).
**Eliminate.** Compare each choice with your prediction and the text. Cross out every choice that has even one wrong part.
**Choose the choice that is fully supported by the text** — not the one that sounds most impressive, and not the one that uses the most words from the passage.

blocks.text: **Why predict first?** The wrong choices are written to sound reasonable. If you read them before you have your own idea, each one pulls you a little. If you already have a prediction, the wrong choices lose most of their power.

**How to eliminate well.** A correct answer must be right in **every part**. So look for the one word that kills a choice: an extreme word (always, never, only, completely), a detail that the passage does not mention, a relationship that is reversed. One wrong part means the whole choice is wrong.
4. The trap-answer families
The wrong answers on the SAT are not random. They usually belong to a small number of families. Learn their names: when you can name the trap, you stop falling into it.

rows: Talks about a bigger topic than the passage covers.
Passage about one study of desert ants → choice: "Insects are well adapted to harsh environments."
True, but only one detail; not the main point.
Main idea question → choice repeats the number of ants tested.
Uses absolute words the passage does not support: always, never, only, all, completely, proves.
The first part is correct, the second part is wrong (or the other way round).
"The library had the most visitors in both years, and its visitors increased" — the first half is true, the second is false.
Says the reverse of the passage, often by missing a word like not or however.
Passage: the result surprised researchers → choice: "confirmed what researchers expected."
A true statement (even from the passage) that does not answer the question asked.
The question asks what weakens a claim → choice is a fact that supports it.
Repeats a word from the passage but with a different meaning or in the wrong role.
Passage mentions "weight" of a bridge → choice "heaviness" for a blank that needs "economy."

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: A choice that copies many words from the passage is not safer. The word-match trap is designed to catch students who match words instead of meaning.
Extreme words are rarely right: SAT passages, especially science passages, usually make careful claims (may, suggests, some, often).
Read the whole choice: half-right answers become wrong in their last few words.
A true fact is not automatically the right answer; it must answer the exact question in the stem.

blocks.text: 5. Guessing — always answer
There is **no penalty for wrong answers**, so a blank answer is always a lost chance. If you must guess:

items: Eliminate any choice with an extreme word, an off-topic idea or a grammar rule you know is broken.
Between the remaining choices, prefer the one that is closest to the passage's actual wording **and** meaning.
In the last minute of the module, make sure every question has an answer, even if you have not read it.

blocks.text: 6. What to do in Module 2

items: **Do not judge your performance from how Module 2 feels.** If it feels hard, that usually means Module 1 went well.
**Stay with the two-pass method.** Harder modules have more questions that need 90+ seconds, so marking and moving on matters even more.
**Expect better traps.** In a harder module, wrong choices are closer to the right answer. Your prediction and careful elimination are your protection.
**Remember that Module 1 is closed.** Do not think about questions you may have missed there; focus only on the screen in front of you.
**Leave the last 3–4 minutes** for the marked questions and to check that nothing is blank.

blocks.title: اسم الفخ = نص الحل
blocks.text: كل إجابة غلط في الـSAT ليها "عيلة": أوسع من النص (too broad)، أضيق من النص (too narrow)، متطرّفة بكلمات زي always وonly، نصها صح ونصها غلط (half-right)، عكس المعنى (opposite)، معلومة صح بس مش هي المطلوبة (true but irrelevant)، أو فيها نفس كلمة النص بمعنى تاني (word-match). لما تسمّي الفخ، عمرك ما هتقع فيه تاني.
Worked examples
Watch the method work. Each example shows the prediction, then the trap name for every wrong choice.

**Example 1 — Main idea.** "For years, city planners in many countries believed that adding more lanes to a crowded road would reduce traffic jams. Studies of road expansions, however, have repeatedly found that within a few years the wider roads become just as crowded as before, because the extra space encourages more people to drive. Some planners now argue that improving buses and trains is a more effective way to reduce traffic."

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?  A) Wider roads always lead to more traffic accidents.  B) Adding lanes may not reduce traffic for long, because it can attract more drivers.  C) Many people prefer driving to taking buses and trains.  D) Some studies of road expansions lasted a few years.

**Prediction before the choices:** "More lanes don't fix traffic for long — they bring more drivers." **Answer: B**, which matches the prediction and keeps the careful word "may." **A** is off-topic and extreme (accidents are never mentioned; "always"). **C** is true but irrelevant: the passage does not discuss people's preferences. **D** is too narrow: a small detail about the studies, not the main idea.

**Example 2 — Inference with an extreme trap.** "In a laboratory test, tomato plants that were exposed to recordings of buzzing bees released more pollen than plants kept in silence. The researchers caution that the test used only one tomato variety and that real bees produce vibrations as well as sound."

Which choice is best supported by the text?  A) Recordings of bees can fully replace real bees on tomato farms.  B) The sound of buzzing may affect pollen release in at least one tomato variety, but more testing is needed.  C) Tomato plants are unable to release pollen in silence.  D) Real bees produce more pollen than tomato plants.

**Prediction:** "Buzzing sound seems to increase pollen release, but the result is limited." **Answer: B.** **A** is extreme ("fully replace") and ignores the researchers' caution. **C** is extreme and opposite: plants in silence released less pollen, not none. **D** is a word-match trap: it reuses "real bees" and "pollen" in a statement that makes no sense from the passage.

**Example 3 — Using the two-pass method.** You are on question 15 at minute 15. It is a two-passage question and after 90 seconds you are torn between B and D. **Correct move:** choose the one with better support (say, D), mark it for review, and go on. At minute 29 you finish question 27 and return. Reading the passages again, you notice that Text 2 says "some" while choice D says "most" — so you switch to B for a clear textual reason. That is exactly how the second pass should work.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Stem first → whole passage → predict → eliminate → choose.
Checkpoints: question 7 at 8 minutes, question 14 at 16, question 21 at 24.
Over 90 seconds and still unsure: best guess, mark for review, move on.
Name the trap for every choice you eliminate.
Last minute: no blanks.

blocks.text: Practice
Ten mixed questions in real test format. Use the full method on each one: predict first, then eliminate. The explanations at the end name the trap in every main wrong choice.

blocks.title: Strategy practice: 10 mixed questions
blocks.intro: Untimed. For each question: read the stem, read the whole passage, predict, eliminate, choose. Then check which trap caught you in the explanations.

questions.p: Many people assume that bees find flowers mainly by color and scent. Entomologist Rhea Okafor investigated another possibility: that bumblebees can sense the weak electric fields around flowers. In her trials, bees landed on artificial flowers carrying a small electric charge more often than on identical uncharged flowers. Okafor suggests that electric signals may also help bees tell whether a flower has recently been visited by another bee.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Bumblebees choose flowers by color alone.
Insects use many different senses to survive in their habitats.
Bumblebees may use electric fields, in addition to color and scent, to gather information about flowers.
Okafor used artificial flowers in her trials.
questions.e: The passage presents Okafor's evidence that bees sense electric fields as an extra source of information. "Color alone" is the opposite trap, "insects use many senses" is too broad, and the artificial flowers are a true but too narrow detail.

questions.p: In a survey of 400 secondary-school students in Alexandria, those who read for pleasure at least three times a week scored higher, on average, on a vocabulary test than those who rarely read for pleasure. The researchers point out, however, that the survey cannot show whether reading caused the higher scores, since students who already have larger vocabularies may simply enjoy reading more.
questions.q: Based on the text, which choice best describes the researchers' conclusion?
c: The survey shows a link between reading for pleasure and vocabulary scores but does not prove that one causes the other.
Reading for pleasure is the only way to build a strong vocabulary.
Reading for pleasure definitely causes higher vocabulary scores.
Students in Alexandria read more than students in other cities.
questions.e: The researchers find a link but warn that the cause is unclear. "The only way" is an extreme trap, "definitely causes" is the opposite of their warning, and other cities are never compared (off-topic).

questions.p: The new pedestrian bridge was praised not for its beauty but for its ______: the engineers removed every element that did not help carry weight, producing a structure that used 30% less steel than earlier designs.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: ornamentation
complexity
heaviness
economy
questions.e: Removing everything unnecessary and using less steel describes economy (careful use of resources). "Ornamentation" and "complexity" are opposite traps, and "heaviness" is a word-match trap built from "weight" in the passage.

questions.p: Most desert plants survive by storing water in thick leaves or stems. The welwitschia of the Namib Desert, ______, has only two long, thin leaves, and scientists believe it can absorb moisture from the coastal fog that drifts over the desert.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: for instance,
however,
as a result,
in addition,
questions.e: The welwitschia is different from "most desert plants," so a contrast is needed. "For instance" would wrongly present it as an example of plants with thick water-storing leaves (opposite relationship); "as a result" and "in addition" suggest cause and addition that the text does not show.

questions.p:
Library | Visitors in 2022 | Visitors in 2024
North Library | 18,000 | 24,000
River Library | 30,000 | 27,000
Hill Library | 12,000 | 21,000

A city council report claims that the evening opening hours introduced at all three public libraries in 2023 increased the number of visitors at every library. The data in the table, however, do not fully support this claim, since ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?
c: River Library had fewer visitors in 2024 than in 2022.
Hill Library had more visitors in 2024 than in 2022.
River Library had the most visitors in both years, and its number of visitors grew.
North Library had more visitors than Hill Library in both years.
questions.e: Only a library whose visitors fell weakens the claim, and River fell from 30,000 to 27,000. Hill's increase is true but supports the claim (true but irrelevant), the River choice with "grew" is half-right, and the North–Hill comparison is true but irrelevant.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Aswan High Dam on the Nile was completed in 1970.
• It controls the river's yearly flooding.
• It produces hydroelectric power.
• Lake Nasser, the reservoir behind the dam, is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world.
• Building the dam required moving the ancient temples of Abu Simbel to higher ground.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize a cultural cost of building the dam. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The Aswan High Dam controls the Nile's yearly flooding and produces hydroelectric power.
Lake Nasser, behind the Aswan High Dam, is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world.
Completed in 1970, the Aswan High Dam was built on the Nile.
Building the Aswan High Dam, which was completed in 1970, required moving the ancient temples of Abu Simbel to higher ground.
questions.e: Only the move of the ancient temples is a cultural cost. Flood control and electricity are benefits (true but irrelevant to the goal), the lake's size is off-goal, and the last choice gives general facts with no cost at all.

questions.p: The collection of letters written by the explorer's crew members ______ now kept in a climate-controlled archive at the national library.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: are
were
is
have been
questions.e: The subject is "collection" (singular), so the singular verb "is" is needed; "now" also requires the present. "Are" and "have been" fall into the nearest-noun trap by agreeing with "letters" or "members," and "were" is plural and past.

questions.p: Every morning Grandfather Selim opened his shop at exactly seven, though customers rarely came before nine. __He swept the front step, polished the brass scale, and turned each spice jar so that its label faced the street.__ To his grandson, this routine seemed pointless; to Selim, it was the reason the shop had survived for forty years.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It gives specific details of a routine that the text later presents as important to the character.
It explains why customers rarely came to the shop before nine.
It shows that the grandson had taken over the shop's daily work.
It describes the history of the spice trade in the town.
questions.e: The sentence lists the details of Selim's morning routine, which the last sentence says he values deeply. It gives no reason for the late customers (unsupported), the grandson does not do the work (opposite: he finds it pointless), and the history of the spice trade is too broad.

questions.p: The painting's colors are muted and its subject is an ordinary kitchen table, yet its composition is so arresting that visitors often stop in the doorway of the gallery before they have even stepped inside.
questions.q: As used in the text, what does the word "arresting" most nearly mean?
c: detaining
striking
calming
confusing
questions.e: Something arresting catches attention strongly, which is why visitors stop and look: "striking." "Detaining" is the secondary-meaning (word-match) trap from the police sense of "arrest"; "calming" and "confusing" are not supported by the text.

questions.p: Archaeologists working in Egypt's Faiyum region found grains of wheat and barley in storage pits that are about 7,000 years old. In the same layers of soil, they also found many fish bones and the bones of wild animals. These findings suggest that the early people who lived at the site ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: had completely stopped hunting once they began to grow crops.
were the first people in the world to grow wheat and barley.
combined farming with fishing and hunting rather than relying on a single source of food.
stored their fish in the same pits as their grain.
questions.e: Grain plus fish and wild-animal bones in the same layers points to a mixed diet. "Completely stopped hunting" is the opposite of the evidence, "first in the world" is extreme and unsupported, and storing fish in the grain pits is a word-match trap: the bones were in the same soil layers, not the same pits.

blocks.title: Remember
items: About 71 seconds per question on average: fast on grammar and transitions, slower on inference and evidence.
Two passes: answer, or guess + mark for review + move on; return to marked questions at the end.
Always predict before reading the choices, then eliminate any choice with one wrong part.
Seven trap families: too broad, too narrow, extreme, half-right, opposite, true but irrelevant, word-match.
No penalty for wrong answers: never leave a blank. In Module 2, stay calm and keep the same method.
